title: Ten minutes of compassion
hook: put the compassion research into one sit

segments.voice: Yesterday: caring for yourself as a carer. Your line was me too, because compassion includes the one doing the caring. Did the rest happen, even a short one? Day one thousand three hundred twenty-two.

Here's a challenge for a single sit. For the last stretch of days, this path has piled up findings about compassion. Feeling another's pain can swamp you. Warmth and a wish to help hold up better. Carers wear out. The skill can be trained, and it can widen to people unlike you. And it has to include the person doing it. Findings are useful, but you can't sit with a finding on a Tuesday night. So today the whole pile goes into one practice. And an old practice already exists for exactly this, with a set order of people and a short line to say to each. That line is today's carry.
screen: `A PILE OF FINDINGS.` → `ONE SIT TO HOLD THEM.` → `AN OLD ORDER, A SHORT LINE.`

segments.voice: First, the picture, back from the day on bias. The short discourse on loving-kindness in the Sutta Nipata gives one image to aim at: a mother guarding her only child, held as a boundless heart toward every living being. The Pali word is metta, usually translated loving-kindness. Second, the order. A Theravada manual called the Path of Purification, which tradition credits to the commentator Buddhaghosa, lays the practice out in steps. Yesterday it supplied the starting point. Here is the whole route. Begin with yourself. Then someone dear. Then someone neutral, a face you pass without a thought. Then someone hostile. The aim, the manual says, is to break down the barriers between these people until the wish is the same for each of them. Third, what the research adds. The studies this path looked at suggest that feeling another's pain can drown you, while warmth and a wish to help hold up better. That is what these phrases do. They don't ask you to feel anyone's pain. They ask you to wish them well. And starting with yourself is yesterday's line, me too, built right into the method. Fourth, when it sticks. Nothing has to be felt on cue. The manual expects resistance, especially at the hostile person, and advises going back to an easier person for a while, then returning. Teachers word the phrases differently; common ones are plain: may you be well, may you be safe, may you be at ease. And the ten minutes? Five stops, two minutes each.
screen: `THE MOTHER AND HER ONLY CHILD.` · `SELF, DEAR, NEUTRAL, HOSTILE.` · `WISH WELL, DON'T DROWN.` · `WHEN IT STICKS, GO BACK.` · then, large: `MAY YOU BE WELL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one quick pass through all five. Settle, and let the breath slow. Start with yourself, a few breaths, silently: may I be well, may I be safe, may I be at ease. Then someone dear: may you be well. Then a neutral face, a cashier or a neighbor whose name you never learned. Then, only if it feels possible, someone difficult; if not, stay with the neutral face a little longer. Last, let the wish go out to everyone at once. If you pray, you can hold these same people in your own prayer instead. The bell holds the time.
Ten minutes of compassion. Loving-kindness in the old manual's order: you, someone dear, someone neutral, someone hard, then everyone. Today's word.

Your line: may you be well. Today, if you can, give it the full ten minutes, two for each of the five. Or just say the line once, silently, to a stranger you pass. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-two.

howItsDone: In loving-kindness practice, Buddhists and others silently repeat short wishes such as "may you be well," moving from themselves to a dear person, a neutral person, a difficult person and finally all beings.

fork.setup: you reach the hostile person in the sequence and your chest tightens. what do you do?
options: push through and force the wish out.
go back to an easier person for a while, then return.
fork.reveal: the Path of Purification expects this. it advises going back to the earlier, easier people for a while, and then turning to the hard one again.

original.note: Pali, from the Buddhist texts: loving-kindness, the warm wish for another's well-being.

trapdoor: what you thought: compassion practice means trying to feel nice.
what it means: a set order that carries one plain wish from you, outward, to everyone.
what a scholar hears: the Path of Purification goes self, dear, neutral, hostile, and aims at breaking down the barriers between them.

sources.work: The Path of Purification (Buddhaghosa, by tradition)

sources.ref: Singer and Klimecki, "Empathy and compassion" (Current Biology)

notes: Confirm the paraphrase of the Karaniya Metta Sutta (Sn 1.8): as a mother would protect her only child with her life, so one should cultivate a boundless mind toward all beings.
Confirm the Visuddhimagga IX sequence (oneself, a dear person, a neutral person, a hostile person) and the aim of 'breaking down the barriers' (simasambheda) between them.
Confirm that Visuddhimagga IX advises returning to the earlier persons when resentment arises toward the hostile person, then returning to the hostile person.
The 'all beings' step at the end is the common modern teaching form; the Visuddhimagga's own extension to all beings comes after the barriers are broken down. Confirm wording.
The phrases 'may I be well / safe / at ease' are described as common modern wordings used by teachers, not a fixed traditional text.
The link to the empathy/compassion research recaps day 1304 (Singer and Klimecki) without new numbers.

Editor pass: the Sutta Nipata image is now framed as a callback to day 1307 (which used it) and shortened; the Visuddhimagga is linked to day 1321; the myth about starting with the hardest person (repeated from day 1321) was replaced with one about the phrases' wording; 'five people' became 'five stops', since the last stop is everyone.
Outline practice is 'practice ten minutes'; the app's sit is two minutes, so the script offers a two-minute pass now and the full ten (five people, two minutes each) later.
